settle: Pedestrian and vehicle volumes on each corridor before and after, which would turn counts into risks per pedestrian. The pandemic emptied Midtown (34th, 42nd and 57th Streets) more than the residential area around 14th Street, so the comparison is confounded by exposure in a direction that favours this result.

research_needed.question: Did risk per pedestrian on 14th Street fall after the busway?
research_needed.data: Pedestrian counts (DOT Bi-Annual Pedestrian Counts include 14th Street sites) and vehicle counts by corridor.
research_needed.design: Crashes per pedestrian-count index, before and after, against comparison corridors.

notes: Persons injured or killed give RR 1.355 (0.922 to 1.991). Against each comparison street alone: 23rd 1.041 (0.628 to 1.725); 34th 1.34 (0.82 to 2.189); 42nd 1.368 (0.86 to 2.176); 57th 1.641 (0.925 to 2.91). In the five months before the pandemic (October 2019 to February 2020 against a year earlier) RR 0.852 (0.315 to 2.305), too few crashes to say anything. Against 23rd Street, the most similar two-way crosstown street outside Midtown, the ratio is close to 1. The data show no safety gain for pedestrians on 14th Street relative to other crosstown streets, and they do not show a loss either once Midtown's emptying during the pandemic is considered.
notes_referee: Referee reproduced RR 1.319 (0.895 to 1.943), stable across buffers 15-45 m. Pre-trend: false-break ratios 1.15 and 1.16. Street-name count gives 0.83. Contested stands.
